hints: Look straight up the 2015 line on the x-axis and count how many of the five lines are at their highest point for the whole 2000 to 2016 period.
Remember that a line graph of percentages over time shows correlation only, it cannot by itself prove what caused a rise or fall, such as overuse or new guidelines.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph actually shows**

Look closely at the axes and key. The y-axis is percentage of resistant bacteria, the x-axis is year, and each line is a different antibiotic. The graph only tells us how resistance changed, not why it changed.

Rule to remember: data shows pattern, not cause.

**Reject any conclusion about cause**

Options A and C both use the word caused. Overuse causing resistance, or guidelines causing a fall, may be true in real life but you cannot prove it from this graph alone. In Cambridge data questions, any causal claim from descriptive data is unsafe.

**Test the pure description statements**

Now check B and D against the lines. For D, compare 2000 and 2016. Tetracycline (solid top line) starts at about $50\%$ in 2000 and ends at about $40\%$ in 2016, so it is lower, not higher. D is false.

For B, look at 2015. Ciprofloxacin, penicillin and cefixime all reach their highest values around 2015 before falling in 2016, while tetracycline peaked earlier in 2014. That is three antibiotics at a peak in 2015, so B fits the data exactly.

options.A: The percentage for ciprofloxacin does rise, but the graph cannot prove overuse caused it. Cause cannot be concluded from trend data alone.
options.B: In 2015, three lines (ciprofloxacin, penicillin and cefixime) are at their maximum values for the period shown, which is a direct description of the data.
options.C: Resistance to some antibiotics does fall from 2015 to 2016, but the graph gives no information about treatment guidelines, so cause cannot be concluded.
options.D: Not true for all five. Tetracycline is lower in 2016 (about 40%) than in 2000 (about 50%), so the statement fails.
